extracted.intended_audience: princes, rulers, and those seeking practical guidance on acquiring and maintaining political power
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for ruling princes on the foundations of states, the proper composition and management of armed forces, and the prudent exercise of virtues and vices to secure and retain power. Emphasizes military preparedness, use of one’s own troops, and pragmatic moral choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundations of a state: good laws and good arms
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief foundations of all states, new as well as old or composite, are good laws and good arms; where the state is not well armed there cannot be good laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machiavelli asserts that arms are primary: 'as there cannot be good laws where the state is not well armed, it follows that where they are well armed they have good laws.' He therefore leaves laws aside to emphasize the necessity of a prince keeping his foundations well laid by ensuring effective military strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on mercenaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercenaries are useless and dangerous; if one holds his state based on these arms, he will stand neither firm nor safe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed anti-patterns: mercenaries are disunited, ambitious, undisciplined, unfaithful, 'valiant before friends, cowardly before enemies'; they fight for pay and not loyalty, rob in peace and flee in war. Historical examples: Italy’s ruin traced to dependence on mercenaries; Charles VIII’s easy advance. Scoring note: reliance on mercenaries is a major strategic weakness and should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware mercenary captains
rubrics_metrics.description: Mercenary captains, whether capable or not, pose grave risks: capable captains will seek their own greatness, and incapable ones will ruin you in the usual way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a mercenary captain is competent he is untrustworthy because he aspires to power (may oppress his master); if incompetent, he brings defeat. Examples: Sforza and Braccio turning ambitions elsewhere; Giovanni Acuto’s uncertain fidelity. Guidance: do not entrust principal command to mercenary captains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince (or republic) must lead/appoint one’s own forces
rubrics_metrics.description: When arms must be resorted to, the prince should go in person as captain; republics should send their citizens, recall unsatisfactory commanders, and secure good ones by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows that states fighting with their own arms (citizens or subjects) make greatest progress; republics armed with citizens resist domination better than those using foreign arms. Examples: Rome, Sparta, and the Swiss as free because they were armed with their own men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliaries are more hazardous than mercenaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliaries (foreign forces lent by another power) may be useful in themselves but are always disadvantageous to he who calls them in: losing makes you undone, winning makes you captive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and anti-patterns: auxiliaries are united and obedient to their native authority, so you become dependent; historical examples include Pope Julius II relying on Ferdinand of Spain and the Emperor of Constantinople using Turks who would not leave — leading to servitude. Recommendation: avoid auxiliaries unless you do not desire conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed armies are inferior to one’s own forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Armies composed partly of mercenaries/foreign auxiliaries and partly national forces are better than mercenaries/auxiliaries alone but much inferior to one’s own troops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: France under Charles VII established national ordinances and infantry; Louis XI later raised Swiss mercenaries which reduced the value of France’s own arms. Mixed armies create dependency and reduce resilience; the wise prince prefers armies made of his own subjects/dependents.

rubrics_metrics.name: One’s own forces are essential to security
rubrics_metrics.description: No principality is secure without having its own forces; reliance on others leaves one dependent on fortune rather than valour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: one’s own forces are composed of subjects, citizens, or dependents. Preparation should follow historical rules (e.g., Philip father of Alexander). Practical implication: build, organize, and maintain national/regime troops rather than hiring foreigners.

rubrics_metrics.name: The art of war is the prince’s principal study
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince ought to have no other aim or thought than war and its rules and discipline; this is the sole art that belongs to him who rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting the art of war leads to loss of state. The prince should study both by action (training, drill, hunting to accustom body, learning terrain) and by study (reading histories of illustrious captains, imitating exemplars such as Cyrus, Alexander, Scipio). In peace, devote more time to martial exercise than in war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical military preparation: drill, reconnaissance, and study of terrain
rubrics_metrics.description: In peace the prince should keep men organized and drilled, follow the chase to learn terrain, and take the greatest care to understand mountains, valleys, plains, rivers, and marshes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of localities serves two uses: defend one’s country and generalize to other regions (terrain similarities). This training permits surprise, selection of quarters, leading armies, arraying battles, and besieging towns to advantage. Practice via continuous discussion of scenarios (Philopoemen example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from history and emulate exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: To exercise the intellect the prince should read histories and study the actions of illustrious men to examine causes of victories and defeats and imitate successful exemplars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to imitate past heroes (Alexander imitating Achilles, Scipio imitating Cyrus). Study Xenophon’s Cyrus as model; learn both military and moral qualities. Use historical analysis to avoid errors and adopt proven practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic morality: know how to do wrong when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince wishing to hold his own must know how to do wrong, and to make use of it or not according to necessity; he should follow real conduct over imaginary virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machiavelli stresses that aiming only at ideal virtues can destroy a ruler; some vices that preserve the state should be embraced if necessary, while avoiding those that would surely lead to ruin. The prince should be sufficiently prudent to avoid vices that would lose his state, and tolerate reputational vices that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer frugality (meanness) to ruinous liberality
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality, when exercised so as to be recognized, injures a prince by draining his resources and forcing burdens on subjects; it is wiser to accept a reputation for meanness so as to retain sufficient revenues to defend and govern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If liberality depletes one’s own property one becomes despised and vulnerable; better to be sparing with one’s own resources and generous with others’ (e.g., conquerors distributing spoils). Examples: Pope Julius II’s thriftiness allowed war without extraordinary taxes; Caesar needed reputation for liberality while rising but must moderate when established. Scoring note: prefer sustainable economics over public displays that jeopardize state finances.

rubrics_metrics.name: On cruelty and clemency: use cruelty prudently to secure order
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince ought to desire to be considered clement, but must not misuse clemency; limited cruelty that secures unity and obedience can be more merciful overall than excessive leniency which permits disorders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cesare Borgia’s cruelty reconciled and pacified the Romagna; Florentines’ leniency led to Pistoia’s destruction. Guidance: be slow to act, temperate, and avoid excess; use punishments to prevent greater communal harms. The prince should balance humanity and firmness.

rubrics_metrics.name: When choosing between being loved or feared, prefer fear without hatred
rubrics_metrics.description: It is much safer to be feared than loved when one cannot have both, because fear depends on the prince’s control and preserves obedience, whereas love depends on subjects’ fickle goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A wise prince should inspire fear but avoid hatred by abstaining from seizing subjects’ property or women and by acting with proper justification when executing. Men are ungrateful and fickle; fear secures obedience. Practical rule: induce dread of punishment but refrain from actions that provoke hatred (property seizure, dishonour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain military discipline through appropriate severity
rubrics_metrics.description: Too much forbearance undermines military discipline and can lead to rebellion; harshness (even inhuman cruelty) combined with valour may hold diverse armies together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hannibal’s cruelty produced unity and fear among heterogeneous forces; Scipio’s forbearance led to mutiny in Spain. When commanding soldiers, it may be necessary to disregard reputation for cruelty to keep an army united and effective. However, always weigh against risk of provoking hatred among subjects.
